newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Argentine soprano channels adversity into art.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Argentine soprano channels adversity into art.

text.p: She dreams of playing the impoverished Mimi, dying of consumption in "La Boheme." But unlike many aspiring sopranos, Argentine Fabiana Bravo brings tragic real-life experience to one of opera's most famous tragic roles.

In her dream, no less a tenor than Luciano Pavarotti plays Rodolfo, whose love for Mimi in Puccini's century-old classic is doomed by their poverty. In reality, Bravo, 26, the youngest of nine children raised by an impoverished family, was a winner of Pavarotti's International Voice Competition in Philadelphia last year, even though her operatic training was modest to say the least.

She is now seeking to win her place on stage and leave behind a past rife with the kind of sorrow dramatised by opera librettists. Deeply scarred by the poverty and death of her parents when she was young, Bravo finds a link between her life and the lyric art.

"There is a lot in common. That is what attracts me so much to opera," she told Reuters, weeping as the adversity of her earlier years flooded back. "I am a sensitive person, very melancholic. I like solitude. And opera has that which is so magical that can transmit all these emotions."

Bravo was the youngest of nine children, three of whom died young, of a boiler-room labourer in the city of Guaymallen in Mendoza province. When she was 11, her uncle took her to a production of Gershwin's Porgy and Bess and young Fabiana left enchanted.
ART CONSIDERED A WASTE OF TIME

But devoting oneself to art in sleepy Guaymallen in the Andean foothills was considered "a waste of time" that would lead one only to starvation, particularly so after her father died of a heart attack when she was 14. A week later, her mother fell into a coma, emerging three years later with advanced cancer from which she died a short time later.

"It was very hard," Bravo recalled. "The important thing was to get by. It was to work and it didn't matter what because when one is in a desperate situation one will do anything." So she worked as a maid, a supermarket cashier and a babysitter.

And through it all, she sang. She began with the chorus in high school, which proved to be a cathartic release from her troubles at home. "I felt liberated. I left all my problems at the door and I was the happiest woman in the world," she said.

Later, at 22, she earned her first income from her voice. And then, with the $40 she made for singing at a wedding and "a lot of illusions," she left for Buenos Aires to audition for a stage version of "Dracula."
"If I would have thought about it much I wouldn't have done it," she said, describing herself as timid.

Bravo was not chosen for "Dracula" but she did land a part in a musical version of "The Hunchback of Notre Dame." She had to work on the side to support herself, selling massage machines at the train station.

After several performances, she had all but given up hope of a professional career and she moved back to Mendoza in early 1995. Returning to Buenos Aires later to collect her belongings, she received a phone call from popular Argentine singer Valeria Lynch, who had shared the stage with Bravo in one performance and who had startling news for her: Pavarotti wanted to hear her sing.

She had never sung opera before and she knew only the libretto to an aria from Puccini's Tosca. The world-famous Italian tenor at first did not like what he heard, but he asked her to perform in the international contest that is designed to encourage young singers.
With only three months of formal training, she managed to be one of 32 winners out of 2,000 contestants. Her category was "Bel Canto," which rewards beautiful sounds.

Bravo now is halfway through a two-year grant to study voice at the Catholic University of America in Washington, where she is also learning theatre, French, Italian and piano. She plans to study German as well.

Next June, she will play the countess neglected by her lecherous husband in Mozart's comedy "The Marriage of Figaro" in Washington's summer festival. In September she will perform in Poulenc's "Les Dialogues des Carmelites" in Washington.
"It's as though there were little angels clearing the way for me to pass," she said with a smile.
